> I just want your heart. The Father just wants your heart. Give Us that, which you already have, and the rest will come in time. 

:::{.callout-tip}
Pikuach nefesh (Hebrew for "saving a soul" or "saving a life") is the supreme foundational principle in Halakha (Jewish law) stating that the preservation of human life overrides virtually any other religious rule, commandment (mitzvah), or restriction in Judaism.
:::


:::{.callout-tip}
In Jewish law (Halakha), an agunah (plural: agunot) literally translates to a "chained" or "anchored" woman. It represents one of the most legally complex and emotionally distressing situations a woman can face within traditional Jewish family law. An agunah is a woman who is legally trapped in her marriage; she is no longer living with her husband, but she is completely forbidden from moving on or remarrying. Read more about the [Agunah problem](https://www.chabad.org/library/article_cdo/aid/613084/jewish/The-Agunah.htm)
:::


## :handshake: Discussion {#sec-discussion}
1. As you watched this episode, which characters or moments stood out to you the most, and why? What was it about those scenes or people that captured your attention?
2. At the end of the previous episode, Jesus sends Simon and Matthew together on the search for Mary Magdalene. What might Jesus hope to accomplish by sending "a fox and a fish" on a mission together? 
3. Why doesn't Jesus just "bring Mary back" (Ramah) or "make food appear out of thin air" (Thomas)? What do you think Mother Mary means when she says that our God is not like Thoth, who could be compelled to grant wishes through rituals?
4. Question from Matthew: "What if you were cut off from Jesus by something in your past, wouldn't you want help getting back to Him as soon as possible?"
5. When Simon and Matthew find Mary, she refuses to return with them. She says: "He already fixed me once... and I broke again. I can't face Him." What do you think Mary is experiencing emotionally and spiritually? Why does she find it so difficult to return to Jesus? How do Simon and Matthew respond?
6. Mother Mary brings Magdalene to Jesus, who is praying in His tent. Mary confesses: *"I'm just so ashamed. You redeemed me, and I just threw it all away. [...] I owe you everything, but I just don't think I can do it. Live up to it. Repay you. How could I leave, how could I go back to the place I was? And I didn't even come back on my own. They had to come get me. I just can't live up to it."* What do you think lies behind Mary's shame? What is she struggling to understand about redemption, grace, and her relationship with Jesus? How does Jesus respond, and what does His response reveal about how He sees her?
7. The episode explores several encounters with the law and its violations: Mary runs away, Jesus heals on the Sabbath, and the disciples pluck grain on the Sabbath. How does Jesus respond in each situation? What do these encounters reveal about His understanding of the law, His priorities, and His identity?

## :thought_balloon: Food for thought {#sec-thought}
1. When you find yourself in a difficult situation, what tends to keep you from turning to Jesus?
2. Mary brags about her win and answes brazenly to the old gambler, only to discover (almost immediately) how foolishly confident she was. Can you think of a time when your own pride, overconfidence, or poor judgment led you into trouble? What did that experience teach you about yourself?
3. Did you note where Matthew got an idea to look at the underground bar (called The Nomad)? "I can't believe I made it up the stairs. Dionysus carried me". Remember what verse Matthew recites when walking down the stairs to The Nomad (and what Jesus told him before they went on the mission)?
4. Thomas says "we're completely out of food" and Jesus replies "seems like something we should seek my Father about." What behavior is Jesus modeling for us here?
